NO!!!!! Please read this: New Orleans filmmaker cleared in cold-case murder; false positive highlights limitations of familial DNA searching

If you want to learn more about your family history, do actual genealogy research. There are a lot of public records out there that can help. This DNA thing is just a razzle-dazzle to get you to give up personally identifying info so you can become part of Ancestry's marketing. They have publicly stated they are moving away from genealogy and into 'people information.' Don't give them your money or your biology.

Also, if you truly are interested in genealogy research, I'd love to assist you. I am very good at it and have traced a lot of my and my spouse's families back many, many generations.

To get started you are going to need a place to put all of your information. There are a lot of programs out there that can help with this. Some free, some cost. This blog post gives you a pretty good idea of that is available, Is there a "best" genealogy program? .

I have tried some of the online ones and don't really like them. I used to use Ancestry's online tree, but since they changed their business model and moved more into the DNA/health info stuff I stopped. I have also tried the worldwide online tree from FamilySearch, but they allow anyone to go in and change 'your' information, which I really dislike. I understand why they do it, as their aim is to have a world-wide family tree, but I'm not that social and don't care. For the last few years, I have been using RootsMagic and really like it. I am using the free version, but find it has sufficient features for my needs.

So - now you have a place to put your info, how do you populate it? One of the best places online for genealogy information is FamilySearch. It is run by the Mormon Church. It's my understanding that their religion requires them to conduct genealogy research so they have made it their mission to make as much genealogy information available for free online. You will be able to spend years searching their records for various family lines. They also have a volunteer system where you can help index records to make them available for others. I have participated in some of those as a way to give back for all the free info. and it's pretty fun and helps hone your skills (on reading the docs for critical info, cursive, etc.)

There are also numerous online libraries, university archives, historic foundations, and document repositories, not to mention the brick and mortal places. Once you have a general idea of the geographic locations for your family lines, seek out the local libraries, courthouses, churches, etc. They will house documents with family information too. Oh yeah, and old newspapers - they can be a huge help with finding old obituaries, wedding announcements, etc.

I have also found that the use of logic is critical for genealogy research. For example, if you find someone you think might be your ancestor but his birth year appears to make it look like his father was only 11 when he had him, it's likely not the right guy. Also, don't lock into spellings. People were far less literate 'back then' and spellings of names varied a lot. My surname is an example - when my GGFIL (great-grandfather in law) migrated to the US, he added an extra 's' to our name. Another use of good logic is geography. People moved around far less than they do now. Large distances between ancestors means lesser of a chance of a linked relationship. Ultimately the lesson is - don't cling to facts you wish would work, but only those you can verify.
